{{Short description|Problem in probability theory}}
{{Probability distribution
  | name       = Coupon collector's problem
  | type       = discrete
  | parameters = <math>n\in\mathbb N</math> &ndash; number of faces on die
  | support    = <math>k\in\mathbb N</math> &ndash; rolls taken for all faces to appear
  | pdf        = <math>\frac{(n-1)^{\{k-1\}}}{n^{k-1}}</math>
  | cdf        = <math>\frac{n^{\{k\}}}{n^k}</math>
  | mean       = <math>nH_n</math>
  | variance   = <math>n^2H^{(2)}_n-nH_n</math>
  | skewness   = <math>\frac{2n^3H^{(3)}_n-3n^2H^{(2)}_n+nH_n}{\left(n^2H^{(2)}_n-nH_n\right)^{3/2}}\ \underset n\sim\ 6^{3/2}2\frac{\zeta(3)}{\pi^3}</math>
  | kurtosis   = <math>\frac{6n^4H^{(4)}_n-12n^3H^{(3)}_n+7n^2H^{(2)}_n-nH_n}{(n^2H^{(2)}_n-nH_n)^2}\sim\frac65</math>
  | pgf        = <math>G(z) = {\frac nz\choose n}^{-1}</math>
  | mgf        = <math>{\frac n{e^t}\choose n}^{-1}</math>
  | char       = <math>{\frac n{e^{it}}\choose n}^{-1}</math>
}}
[[File:Coupon collector problem.svg|thumb|400px|Graph of number of coupons, {{mvar|n}} vs the expected number of trials (i.e., time) needed to collect them all {{math|''E''(''T'')}}]]
In [[probability theory]], the '''coupon collector's problem''' refers to mathematical analysis of "collect all [[coupon]]s and win" contests. It asks the following question: if each box of a given product (e.g., breakfast cereals) contains a coupon, and there are {{mvar|n}} different types of coupons, what is the probability that more than {{mvar|t}} boxes need to be bought to collect all {{mvar|n}} coupons? An alternative statement is: given {{mvar|n}} coupons, how many coupons do you [[Expected value|expect]] you need to draw with [[Sampling (statistics)#Replacement of selected units|replacement]] before having drawn each coupon at least once? The mathematical analysis of the problem reveals that the [[expected value|expected number]] of trials needed grows as <math>\Theta(n\log(n))</math>.{{efn|Here and throughout this article, "log" refers to the [[natural logarithm]] rather than a logarithm to some other base. The use of Θ here invokes [[big O notation]].}} For example, when {{math|1=''n'' = 50}} it takes about 225<ref group=lower-alpha>E(50) = 50(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/50) = 224.9603, the expected number of trials to collect all 50 coupons. The approximation <math>n\log n+\gamma n+1/2</math> for this expected number gives in this case <math>50\log 50+50\gamma+1/2 \approx 195.6011+28.8608+0.5\approx 224.9619</math>.</ref> trials on average to collect all 50 coupons. Sometimes the problem is instead expressed in terms of an {{mvar|n}}-sided die.

==Solution==
===Calculating the expectation===
Let time {{mvar|T}} be the number of draws needed to collect all {{mvar|n}} coupons, and let {{math|''t''<sub>''i''</sub>}} be the time to collect the {{mvar|i}}-th coupon after {{math|''i'' − 1}} coupons have been collected. Then <math>T=t_1 + \cdots + t_n</math>. Think of {{mvar|T}} and {{math|''t''<sub>''i''</sub>}} as [[random variable]]s. Observe that the probability of collecting the {{mvar|i}}-th {{em|new}} coupon is <math>p_i = \frac{n - (i - 1)}{n} = \frac{n - i + 1}n</math>. Therefore, <math>t_i</math> has [[geometric distribution]] with expectation <math>\frac{1}{p_i} = \frac n{n - i + 1}</math>. By the [[Expected value#Properties|linearity of expectations]] we have:

:<math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}(T) & {}= \operatorname{E}(t_1 + t_2 + \cdots + t_n) \\
& {}= \operatorname{E}(t_1) + \operatorname{E}(t_2) + \cdots + \operatorname{E}(t_n) \\
& {}= \frac{1}{p_1} + \frac{1}{p_2} +  \cdots + \frac{1}{p_n} \\
& {}= \frac{n}{n} + \frac{n}{n-1} +  \cdots + \frac{n}{1} \\
& {}= n \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}\right) \\
& {}= n \cdot H_n.
\end{align}
</math>

Here {{math|''H''<sub>''n''</sub>}} is the {{mvar|n}}-th [[harmonic number]]. Using the [[asymptotics]] of the harmonic numbers, we obtain:

:<math>
\operatorname{E}(T)  = n \cdot H_n = n \log n + \gamma n + \frac{1}{2} + O(1/n),
</math>
where <math>\gamma \approx 0.5772156649</math> is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].

Using the [[Markov inequality]] to bound the desired probability:

:<math>\operatorname{P}(T \geq cn H_n) \le \frac{1}{c}.</math>

The above can be modified slightly to handle the case when we've already collected some of the coupons. Let {{mvar|k}} be the number of coupons already collected, then:

:<math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}(T_k) & {}= \operatorname{E}(t_{k+1} + t_{k+2} + \cdots + t_n) \\
& {}= n \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n-k}\right) \\
& {}= n \cdot H_{n-k}
\end{align}
</math>

And when <math>k=0</math> then we get the original result.

===Calculating the variance===
Using the independence of random variables {{math|''t''<sub>''i''</sub>}}, we obtain:

:<math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}(T)& {}= \operatorname{Var}(t_1 + \cdots + t_n) \\
& {} = \operatorname{Var}(t_1) + \operatorname{Var}(t_2) + \cdots + \operatorname{Var}(t_n) \\
& {} = \frac{1-p_1}{p_1^2} + \frac{1-p_2}{p_2^2} +  \cdots + \frac{1-p_n}{p_n^2} \\
& {} = \left(\frac{n^2}{n^2} + \frac{n^2}{(n-1)^2} +  \cdots + \frac{n^2}{1^2}\right) - \left(\frac{n}{n} + \frac{n}{n-1} +  \cdots + \frac{n}{1}\right) \\
& {} = n^2 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1^2} + \frac{1}{2^2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n^2} \right) - n \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n} \right)\\
& {} < \frac{\pi^2}{6} n^2
\end{align}
</math>

since <math>\frac{\pi^2}6=\frac{1}{1^2}+\frac{1}{2^2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n^2}+\cdots</math> (see [[Basel problem]]).

Bound the desired probability using the [[Chebyshev inequality]]:

:<math>\operatorname{P}\left(|T- n H_n| \geq cn\right) \le \frac{\pi^2}{6c^2}.</math>

==Stirling numbers==
Let the random variable {{mvar|X}} be the number of dice rolls performed before all faces have occurred.

The subpower is defined <math>a^{\{b\}}=a!\left\{{b\atop a}\right\}</math>, where <math>\left\{{b\atop a}\right\}</math> is a [[Stirling number of the second kind]].<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Rus|first=Mircea Dan|author-link=Mircea Dan Rus|date=15 January 2025|title=Yet another note on notation|eprint=2501.08762|class=math.NT}}</ref>

Sequences of <math>k</math> die rolls are functions <math>k\rightarrow n</math> counted by <math>n^k</math>, while surjections (that land on each face at least once) are counted by <math>n^{\{k\}}</math>, so the probability that all faces were landed on within the {{mvar|k}}-th throw is <math>P(X\le k)=\frac{n^{\{k\}}}{n^k}</math>. By the recurrence relation of the Stirling numbers, the probability that exactly {{mvar|k}} rolls are needed is <math>P(X=k)=\frac{n^{\{k\}}}{n^k}-\frac{n^{\{k-1\}}}{n^{k-1}}=\frac{(n-1)^{\{k-1\}}}{n^{k-1}}</math>

===Generating functions===
Replacing <math>z</math> with <math>1+z</math> in the [[probability generating function]] produces the o.g.f. for <math>E\left[{X\choose k}\right]</math>. Using the partial fraction decomposition <math>{\frac1x-1\choose n}^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^n{n\choose k}\frac{(-1)^{n-k}}{1-kx}</math>, we can take the expansion
:<math>\begin{aligned}&{\frac n{x+1}\choose n}^{-1}\\
=&\sum_{i=0}^n{n\choose i}\frac{(-1)^{n-i}}{1-i(1-\frac n{x+1+n})}\\
=&\sum_{i=0}^n{n\choose i}(-1)^{n-i}\left(\frac{1+n}{1+n-i}+in\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{(i-1)^{k-1}}{(n+1-i)^{k+1}}x^k\right)\end{aligned}</math>
revealing that for <math>k>0</math>,
:<math>E\left[{X\choose k}\right]=n\sum_{i=0}^n{n\choose i}(-1)^{n-i}i\frac{(i-1)^{k-1}}{(n+1-i)^{k+1}}</math>
Given an o.g.f. {{mvar|f}}, since <math>\left(\frac x{1-x}\right)^i=\sum_{n=0}^\infty{k-1\choose i-1}x^k</math>, a variation of the [[binomial transform]] is <math>[x^k]f\left(\frac x{1+x}\right)=\sum_{i=0}^k{k-1\choose i-1}(-1)^{k-i}[x^i]f(x)</math>. (Specifically, if <math>{\frac n{x+1}\choose n}^{-1}=f\left(\frac x{1+x}\right)</math>, <math>f(x)={n-nx\choose n}^{-1}</math>.)

Rewriting the binomial coefficient via the [[gamma function]] and expanding as the <math>\exp</math> of the [[Polygamma function|polygamma]] series (in terms of [[generalized harmonic number|generalised harmonic numbers]]), we find <math>\left[\frac{x^i}{i!}\right]{n-x\choose n}^{-1}=\sum_{P\in\mathrm{perms}(i)}\prod_{c\in P}H^{(|c|)}_n</math>, so
:<math>E\left[{X\choose k}\right]=\sum_{i=0}^k{k-1\choose i-1}(-1)^{k-i}\frac{n^i}{i!}\sum_{P\in\mathrm{perms}(i)}\prod_{c\in P}H^{(|c|)}_n</math>
which can also be written with the [[falling factorial]] and [[Lah numbers]] as
:<math>E[x^\underline k]=\sum_{i=0}^kL(k,i)(-1)^{k-i}n^i\sum_{P\in\mathrm{perms}(i)}\prod_{c\in P}H^{(|c|)}_n</math>
The [[raw moments]] of the distribution can be obtained from the falling moments via a [[Stirling transform]]; due to the identity <math>\left\{{K\atop i}\right\}(-1)^K=\sum_{k=0}^K\left\{{K\atop k}\right\}L(k,i)(-1)^k</math>, this provides
:<math>E[x^k]=\sum_{i=0}^k\left\{{k\atop i}\right\}(-1)^{k-i}n^i\!\!\sum_{P\in\mathrm{perms}(i)}\prod_{c\in P}H^{(|c|)}_n</math>

==Tail estimates==

A stronger tail estimate for the upper tail can be obtained as follows. Let <math>{Z}_i^r</math> denote the event that the <math>i</math>-th coupon was not picked in the first <math>r</math> trials. Then
:<math>
\begin{align}
P\left [ {Z}_i^r \right ] = \left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^r \le e^{-r / n}.
\end{align}
</math>

Thus, for <math>r = \beta n \log n</math>, we have <math>P\left [ {Z}_i^r \right ] \le e^{(-\beta n \log n ) / n} = n^{-\beta}</math>. Via a union bound over the <math>n</math> coupons, we obtain
:<math>
\begin{align}
P\left [ T > \beta n \log n \right ] = P \left [ 	\bigcup_i {Z}_i^{\beta n \log n} \right ] \le n \cdot P [ {Z}_1^{\beta n \log n} ] \le n^{-\beta + 1}.
\end{align}
</math>

==Extensions and generalizations==
* [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]], but also [[Paul Erdős]] and [[Alfréd Rényi]], proved the limit theorem for the distribution of {{mvar|T}}. This result is a further extension of previous bounds. A proof is found in.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mitzenmacher |first=Michael |title=Probability and computing: randomization and probabilistic techniques in algorithms and data analysis |date=2017 |others=Eli Upfal |isbn=978-1-107-15488-9 |edition=2nd |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom |at=Theorem 5.13 |oclc=960841613}}</ref>

::<math>\operatorname{P}(T < n\log n + cn) \to e^{-e^{-c}}, \text{ as } n \to \infty.</math> which is a [[Gumbel distribution]]. A simple proof by martingales is in .<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kan |first=N. D. |date=2005-05-01 |title=Martingale approach to the coupon collection problem |journal=Journal of Mathematical Sciences |language=en |volume=127 |issue=1 |pages=1737–1744 |doi=10.1007/s10958-005-0134-y |issn=1573-8795}}</ref>
.

* [[Donald J. Newman]] and [[Lawrence Shepp]] gave a generalization of the coupon collector's problem when {{mvar|m}} copies of each coupon need to be collected. Let {{math|''T''<sub>''m''</sub>}} be the first time {{mvar|m}} copies of each coupon are collected. They showed that the expectation in this case satisfies:

::<math>\operatorname{E}(T_m) =  n \log n + (m-1) n \log\log n + O(n), \text{ as } n \to \infty.</math>
:Here {{mvar|m}} is fixed.  When {{math|1=''m'' = 1}} we get the earlier formula for the expectation.

* Common generalization, also due to Erdős and Rényi:

::<math>\operatorname{P}\left(T_m < n\log n + (m-1) n \log\log n + cn\right) \to e^{-e^{-c}/(m-1)!}, \text{ as } n \to \infty.</math>

* In the general case of a nonuniform probability distribution, according to [[Philippe Flajolet]] et al.<ref name="Flajolet">{{citation |first=Philippe |last=Flajolet |first2=Danièle |last2=Gardy |first3=Loÿs |last3=Thimonier |title=Birthday paradox, coupon collectors, caching algorithms and self-organizing search |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |volume=39 |issue=3 |year=1992 |pages=207–229 |doi=10.1016/0166-218x(92)90177-c}}</ref>
::<math>\operatorname{E}(T)=\int_0^\infty \left(1 - \prod_{i=1}^m \left(1-e^{-p_it}\right)\right)dt. </math>

:This is equal to

::<math>\operatorname{E}(T)=\sum_{q=0}^{m-1} (-1)^{m-1-q} \sum_{|J|=q} \frac{1}{1-P_J},</math>

:where {{mvar|m}} denotes the number of coupons to be collected and {{math|''P''<sub>''J''</sub>}} denotes the probability of getting any coupon in the set of coupons {{mvar|J}}.
